events.summary: Full first draft. The page leans into the plant's honest character — quiet, unassuming, tucked behind the Baobab — and finds its interest in the notched leaflets, the etymology, and the edible fruit rather than inflating a modest specimen. No sections manufactured where the plant doesn't earn them (cultural_significance, take_care omitted).

events.notes:
A few reasons I like this direction:
The Oneco story is gold for your page. The historical Palm Society account traces Florida cultivation to Reasoner’s Royal Palm Nursery and says the nursery was probably responsible for the first Florida introduction; seed from those plants was already traveling to Cuba by 1918–19. That is exactly the kind of local connection we usually wish we could find.
The plant itself is genuinely compact. UF/IFAS gives it a typical Florida landscape size of about 12 × 6 feet, calls out its upright form and spiny petioles, and notes that it is a single-stem feather palm. The Brazilian palm guide gives wild stems about 1–4 m tall, persistent leaf bases and conspicuous large teeth on the petiole/sheath margins.
Its native story is more specific than just “Brazil.” Brazil’s official conservation assessment describes it as an endemic of the Atlantic Forest, especially restinga vegetation, and currently assesses it as Least Concern. Kew gives the accepted range from Pernambuco to northern Espírito Santo.
And the fruit really is edible; both the old Florida account and a current UF/IFAS edible-palms publication record Arikury fruit as food.
The one section I’d be most willing to shorten later is cultural_significance, because we have so much unusually good local history that I indulged it a little. But for a first cut, I think the Manatee County connection deserves the space.

Yes — and Claude found some nice visual material, but I would absolutely bring the Oneco/Reasoner history back in. That is too good and too locally relevant to lose. I’d also keep Claude’s “quiet palm behind the Baobab” characterization rather than trying to make this little palm sound grander than it is.
